passage: On the school terrace in Ahmedabad, Arnab and Kalyani sat eating samosas after what Kalyani now called the Great Text Disaster. 'Okay, rule one,' Kalyani said, licking chutney off her thumb. 'If a message feels weird, we ask "what did you mean?" before replying.' 'Rule two,' Arnab said. 'If it still feels off, we call. No essays.' 'Rule three: if I'm upset, I wait before I reply. Even ten minutes.' Arnab nodded. 'Texts are just letters. They don't have faces.' They pinned the rules in their chat. That night Arnab got a message from Kalyani: 'ok.' His thumb hovered. Then he grinned and typed, 'what did you mean? 😄' 'I MEANT OK,' she wrote back, with three laughing faces.

qa.q: Where did Arnab and Kalyani sit eating samosas?

qa.q: Why did Arnab grin before typing 'what did you mean?'

qa.q: Which of their three rules might matter most when someone is hurt, and why?
qa.a: Waiting before replying, because a pause stops a hurt reaction from turning a small misreading into a real fight.

qa.a: She seems amused and reassured, replying in capitals with laughing faces, glad the habit is working.
